newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Despite Vanunu, no nuclear debate in Israel.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Despite Vanunu, no nuclear debate in Israel.

text.p: The public debate which Mordechai Vanunu hoped to inspire has failed to materialise in the 11 years since he spilled Israel's nuclear secrets over the pages of a British newspaper.

A former low-level technician at Israel's ultra-secret atomic bomb factory, Vanunu revealed details and pictures of Israel's Dimona plant to Britain's Sunday Times, he said, to "inform the Israeli people" what their government was doing.
Instead, the authorities have demonised the jailed 45-year-old Israeli and his countrymen have condemned him as a traitor.

Issues debated vehemently in other nuclear countries have never been raised publicly in Israel: Where does it bury its nuclear waste? Where does it store its nuclear warheads? Is the 40-year-old Dimona plant safe?

"Public debate on the nuclear issue in Israel does not exist -- zero," said 50-year-old Israeli film maker Nissim Mossek, the chief video editor for Reuters in Jerusalem whose documentary on Vanunu has its debut this month at the Jerusalem Film Festival.

The hour-long film, called "I Am Your Spy", draws mainly on letters from prison and an interview with Vanunu's brother to paint a portrait of a man few Israelis would recognise: a pensive intellectual with firm ideological motives who views his imprisonment in the tradition of the Christian ethos he adopted -- as the price he must pay for the sins of others.
"LET MY PEOPLE KNOW"

Vanunu is serving an 18-year sentence for espionage and treason, convicted in an Israeli court after Mossad secret service agents abducted him in Rome and spirited him on a ship to Israel. He is held in solitary confinment and gets his first chance at parole next year.
He worked for nine years at Israel's most secret facility, the nuclear reactor in the southern desert town of Dimona, while studying philosophy in neighbouring Beersheba.

By 1986 Vanunu had had enough of both. After completing his MA thesis on Nietzsche, Sartre and Socrates and, by his own admission, helping enrich enough uranium for Israel to build up to 200 nuclear bombs, he left the country.
Vanunu's conversion to Christianity at a church in Australia helped shape his resolve to blow the whistle on Dimona -- a kind of atonement for acting as a cog in Israel's nuclear wheel.

"My action was (taken) to inform the Israeli people. In this nuclear age, everyone has the right to information. Even the most democratic states still try to guard their nuclear secrets. Let my people know," wrote Vanunu in a letter from prison quoted in the film.

Details and pictures which Vanunu gave The Sunday Times thwarted decades of deliberate Israeli ambiguity over Dimona, described to the world when it was built in the 1950s as a textile plant and later as a non-military reactor.
But Vanunu's disclosures failed to spark debate in a country where nuclear armament has never made the public agenda.
"He was a really bad man to do that," says one Beersheba woman in Mossek's film, summing up Israeli sentiment for a man who dared violate the most sensitive of all security taboos.
Many Israelis view nuclear weapons as the last line of defence for a country surrounded by enemies -- and an insurance policy against a repeat of the World War Two Nazi Holocaust.
"The Israeli people are not yet disillusioned with their nuclear policy as I think they should be," said fellow whistle blower Daniel Ellsberg at a Tel Aviv conference on Vanunu earlier this year.
"To this day they haven't really heard enough discussion in this country to understand the dangers that their nuclear policy is posing," he said.
"THE ISRAELI PUBLIC WILL ASK FOR MY FORGIVENESS"
Mossek said an official smear campaign against Vanunu, aided by the local press, helped abort public discourse.
"Everything they published about Vanunu came from the Shin Bet," (Israel's secret internal security agency), he said, citing reports that Vanunu was mentally unstable and even sexually impotent.

Mossek insisted Vanunu was not paid by The Sunday Times as charged in the Israeli press. He said Vanunu's solitary confinement was aimed at driving him crazy and that the former technician had no more secrets to reveal.
Prison officials counter that Vanunu turned down an offer to share a cell with a convicted spy.
"I fully believe that the truth about my actions will be revealed and the Israeli public will ask for my forgiveness. This day will come," Vanunu wrote in a letter from prison.
That day appears a long way off.
